This could reflect cerebellar dysfunction, sensory ataxia (e.g., dorsal column disease), or vestibular pathology. Given the Crohn disease context, key considerations include nutritional deficiencies (e.g., B12, thiamine, copper), medication side effects (e.g., anti-TNF agents rarely associated with demyelination), or inflammatory CNS complications (e.g., neurosarcoidosis, MS-like syndromes). First, I need to characterize the ataxia more precisely — is it cerebellar (e.g., limb dysmetria, nystagmus) or sensory (e.g., worsening in dark, Romberg sign)? Also, assess for associated neurological symptoms (e.g., numbness, weakness, diplopia, dysarthria) and review medications and disease activity.

[QUERY] Have you noticed any other new symptoms along with the unsteady walking—such as numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, double vision, slurred speech, muscle weakness, or difficulty with fine hand movements?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall noticing any other new symptoms like numbness, tingling, double vision, slurred speech, or difficulty with fine hand movements—only the unsteady walking and the weakness in my right upper limb.

[THOUGHT] The patient now reports new right upper limb weakness in addition to gait ataxia. This lateralized motor deficit—combined with truncal and gait ataxia—raises concern for a structural or inflammatory lesion affecting the cerebellum, brainstem, or cervical spinal cord (e.g., demyelinating plaque, compressive lesion, or paraneoplastic/inflammatory process). Given Crohn disease, we must consider both immune-mediated neuroinflammation (e.g., CNS sarcoidosis, MS, ADEM) and complications of chronic inflammation or treatment (e.g., vitamin deficiencies, drug-induced neurotoxicity). Next, I need to assess for red-flag features: timing (acute vs. subacute), progression pattern, associated systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, rash), and current Crohn disease activity (e.g., recent flares, hospitalizations, biologics use). Also, clarify whether the “weakness” is focal (e.g., arm drift, grip weakness) or more diffuse.

[QUERY] When did the right upper limb weakness start relative to the walking difficulty—did it begin at the same time, before, or after? And can you describe the weakness more specifically: for example, does your right arm feel heavy, does it drift downward when held out, or do you have trouble lifting objects or holding things?

Since objective neurological signs are critical in ataxia + focal weakness, the next step is to perform a targeted physical examination. Specifically, I need to assess for cerebellar signs (e.g., finger-nose-finger, heel-shin, dysmetria, nystagmus), Romberg test (to screen for sensory ataxia), limb strength grading (MRC scale), and presence of long tract signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, Babinski). The combination of ipsilateral limb ataxia and weakness points toward a lesion in the contralateral cerebellum (e.g., cerebellar hemisphere infarct/tumor) or, more likely given bilateral gait involvement, a midline cerebellar or brainstem lesion (e.g., vermis, pons). [DIAGNOSIS]  
Progressive Multifocal Encephalopathy (PML)
